extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers interested in narrative technique and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for employing or identifying the stream-of-consciousness narrative mode: representing the flow of a character's thoughts and impressions (often as interior monologue) and its variants across literature and other media. Useful for writers learning the technique and students/critics analyzing examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict multitudinous thoughts and feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to 'depict the multitudinous thoughts and feelings which pass through the mind' of a narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central aim of the technique: portray the flow of subjective experience rather than an externally organized account. Examples include passages from Joyce's Ulysses and Woolf's novels; the technique often foregrounds immediacy and interiority rather than plot-driven exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usually present as an interior monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream of consciousness is usually in the form of an interior monologue which is disjointed or has irregular punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, present thoughts 'directly' without a summarizing narrator. The style may use long, run-on clauses, abrupt shifts, and minimal punctuation to mimic thought. Anti-pattern: converting interior experience into neat, fully punctuated summary — that becomes interior summary, not stream-of-consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological vs literary distinction (subject matter vs technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxford Dictionary distinction: 'in a psychological sense, stream of consciousness is the subject matter, while interior monologue is the technique for presenting it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to decide whether you're aiming to represent the raw flow of consciousness (subject matter) or to present it via a particular narrative device (interior monologue). A piece can deal with stream-like mental life without using interior monologue, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior monologue may be restricted or unbounded
rubrics_metrics.description: While an interior monologue always presents a character's thoughts 'directly', it 'does not necessarily mingle them with impressions and perceptions, nor does it necessarily violate the norms of grammar, or logic' — in contrast to stream-of-consciousness technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can choose degrees of intensity: from organized, grammatical interior monologue (focused, rational thought) to full stream-of-consciousness (half-thoughts, impressions, associative leaps). Be deliberate about where on that spectrum you want your passage to sit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mingle impressions and perceptions; violate grammar/logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The stream‑of‑consciousness technique 'also does one or both of these things' — mingle thoughts with impressions and perceptions and/or violate grammatical or logical norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include sensory impressions interwoven with thought, non-linear associations, syntactic fragmentation, neologisms, and deliberate grammatical breaches to mimic mental flow. Example: Joyce's unpunctuated passages in Ulysses. Anti-pattern: sanitizing these elements so much that the distinctive 'flow' is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use free association and abandon strict chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers may 'abandon strict linear time to record the internal consciousness' and favor free association over chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flashbacks, associative leaps, dreamlike transitions, and collapsing temporal order help reproduce consciousness. Historical precursors (Dujardin, Poe, Tolstoy) and modernists (Joyce, Woolf) demonstrate varying uses. Avoid forcing chronological coherence where the interior logic requires associative movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend narrative modes (authorial description, free indirect style, soliloquy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream-of-consciousness prose often alternates or mixes modes: authorial description, free indirect style, indirect or direct interior monologue, and soliloquy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joyce, Woolf and others mix external viewpoint and interiority; writers can shift between omniscient description and interior passages to frame or contrast consciousness. Use such shifts intentionally to control reader access and tonal effect; abrupt, unmarked shifts can be disorienting if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary syntactic density (long sentences, qualifiers, anxious discursiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early examples show 'long sentences with multiple qualifiers and expressions of anxiety' as characteristic of an associative, anxious interior voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence length and density to reflect mental states: breathless long sentences for associative overflow, terse fragments for shock or clarity. Example: John Neal's early usage and many modernist passages. Beware of reader fatigue from excessive, unrelieved density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ dreamlike, associative, or highly allusive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream-of-consciousness writing can be 'dreamlike' and rely on literary allusions and free dream associations, sometimes pushing conventional plot and character construction to the limit (e.g., Finnegans Wake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagery, puns, allusion, and associative leaps to evoke unconscious or semi-conscious thought. This can sacrifice conventional intelligibility for experiential effect; use when your artistic aim is immersion rather than straightforward narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Can be achieved via multiple techniques across media
rubrics_metrics.description: The term has been adopted to describe similar techniques in poetry, songwriting and film; song lyrics and film dialogue/documentary narration use stream-of-consciousness methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt techniques (unpunctuated phrasing, associative sequencing, voiceover interior monologue) to the affordances of the medium: rhythm and line breaks in poetry/lyrics; voiceover, montage, and editing in film. Examples: songwriters (Sun Kil Moon, Courtney Barnett), Terrence Malick films, and documentary narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reminiscence-focused interiority from stream-of-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers (e.g., Proust) focus on 'the reminiscent aspect of consciousness' — deliberately recapturing past to communicate — and thus may not be performing stream-of-consciousness in the modernist sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the interior passages are organized around deliberate recollection and authorial shaping rather than spontaneous associative flow, label them as reminiscence or reflective interiority rather than pure stream-of-consciousness. This distinction helps set stylistic and structural expectations for readers and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vernacular and dialect to register voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some practitioners mix stream-of-consciousness with vernacular speech (e.g., James Kelman's use of Glaswegian vernacular) to convey authentic mindscape and social voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating dialect, idiom, or vernacular grammar can root interiority in social and linguistic identity, enhancing realism and voice. Be attentive to readability and audience access; use orthography and spelling choices consciously to balance authenticity and comprehension.
